turn_text: Now, what would you say is the most challenging aspect about governing?

working with the legislature, right? During my first two years as governor, both the Ohio House and the Ohio Senate were controlled by Republicans. And we worked together really well. Every week I had the Speaker of the House and the Leader of the Senate come to my office. I put a big round table in my office. And I did that because when you use a round table, there's no head position, right? Everybody's equal. Every week we met, and we debated and we argued and we reached compromise and we got things done. For example, as I said, we passed an energy bill in Ohio, a very strong, renewable standard. Now that was very significant for Ohio because we're a big manufacturing state and we use a lot of energy, but we were able to come to compromise and we got that renewable standard in place We passed significant education reform and the Education Commission of the States, made up of all the states, said that Ohio's education reform was the boldest, most creative in the entire country. So we got things. And then the recession hit, the Great Recession. And that made it really tough. And my final two years, The Democrats had captured control of the House. The Senate remained Republican, and it was just gridlock. We just couldn't get the kind of worker relationship that we had during my first two years. And Ohio, like the rest of the country, was greatly damaged by that recession, and people were hurting. coming to terms with falling revenue, you ask what was most difficult. I said working with the legislature, but I guess dealing with the budget may have been the most because we had falling revenue and increased need. And that's what happens in a recession. And so you have to find ways to try to keep the budget in balance, which is required by our Ohio Constitution. And so you had to find where you're going to try to save money while continuing to fund the most essential things that are important to people. And so I ended up with your votes that I needed at the end of that election.

turn_text: Now, what advice would you give to someone who is starting up in politics?

You know, thank you for asking me that question because I get that question a lot from young people. And the first thing I say is I would not suggest that you try to enter politics as I did, losing in 76, losing in 78, and then losing and then winning again. Because there's no way to learn politics like working in a political campaign. You can read about it in books, but unless you get in there and do the grubby work, make the phone calls, do all of that, those things that you've got to do in a campaign. You can't really understand what a campaign is like, and some people just don't like that kind of experience. Others feed upon it and love it and get excited about it and so on and so forth.
